results.title: When is a DSMB needed? - One UNC Clinical Research
results.content: Home / Resources / Services / Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) / When is a DSMB needed? **A Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) is typically needed in the following situations:**. * All Phase III studies require a DSMB, except for low risk behavioral and nutritional studies. * Phase II multicenter, randomized trials require a DSMB, with the exception of low risk behavioral and nutritional studies. * Phase II trials deemed high risk require a DSMB. + As a general rule, DSMBs are necessary for clinical trials involving diseases with high mortality or morbidity, high risk interventions, and large, multicenter trials. * Single-center open-label Phase I and II clinical trials typically do not require a DSMB, as the local investigator has access to all the data. * For multicenter, high-risk Phase I clinical trials, a DSMB is generally not necessary if there are clear guidelines for stopping the trial. For example, a classic open-label dose escalation trial with objective criteria for halting dose escalation in the event of unacceptable side effects may not need a DSMB. However, if the Data and Safety Monitoring Plan (DSMP) lacks objective criteria, a DSMB may be requested. * A DSMB may not be feasible for clinical trials that are expected to enroll participants too quickly for the formation of a DSMB or for completing thorough data and safety monitoring. If you plan to use the UNC-CH DSMB to monitor a clinical trial funded by an NIH or other federal grant, please submit a copy of your grant proposal to the DSMB for review before submitting it to the funding agency. The DSMB will provide guidance on study stopping rules, appropriate study design, and the safety monitoring plan. If the DSMB agrees to oversee the trial, a letter of support outlining the DSMB’s role in monitoring the study will be provided. If you have questions about whether a DSMB is needed for your study or would like to discuss your research proposal to determine if the UNC-CH DSMB is the right resource, contact Katie Marsh. A meeting can be scheduled to review the details of your research protocol and develop a plan for monitoring study data and ensuring participant safety.

results.title: Decades of underpowered RCT - research methods - Datamethods Discussion Forum
results.content:
Title: Decades of underpowered RCT - research methods - Datamethods Discussion Forum
To Frank’s comment, I generally agree, albeit the reality is the need to have an experienced statistician involved in the study design and execution to implement a priori interim stopping rules, whether frequentist (e.g. using conditional power) or Bayesian (e.g. using predicted probability of success), and then to have an experienced DMC/DSMB convened with reasonable pre-specified thresholds to engage in decision making during closed (executive) sessions when presented with the data. Of course, the budget for the study via whatever the funding entity is, industry or otherwise, still needs to be sufficient to cover the full costs of the study, including the DMC/DSMB, should it go to completion, presuming proper a priori power/sample size estimates were done, which is yet another issue…. Without going into details, in one example of a PIII pivotal trial with formal interim stopping rules, with 3 pre-defined interim analysis time points and conditional power thresholds, and in the absence of clear safety concerns, the trend in conditional power was not favorable for the study over the multiple interim analyses. If the recommendation by the DMC/DSMB is purely based upon the poor trajectory of enrollment, in the absence of clear safety concerns as above, and the sponsor has already engaged in various attempts to improve enrollment, then a recommendation may be made to stop the study because the risk/benefit consideration is no longer favorable. Depending upon the direction and magnitude of the treatment effect in the observed endpoint data versus the pre-study assumptions, the two approaches above can lead to optimistic versus conservative views of the probability of study success and enable the DMC/DSMB to consider the totality of the information to facilitate their decision to continue or to stop the study. In essence, you might increase the study sample size to retain the desired pre-study power assumptions, given that the study would then be likely to reject the null, rather than risking the study ending with an inconclusive result. This would generally be in the context where the treatment effect size likely to be observed in the study may be smaller than hypothesized pre-study, perhaps because that assumption was optimistic, but the interim data show a treatment effect size that is still clinically meaningful.

results.title: Psychometrics of the self-report Concise Associated ...
results.content: Hersh Chair for Depression Research and Clinical Care, Betty Jo Hay Distinguished Chair in Mental Health, Director, Center for Depression Research and Clinical Care, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Phone: 214-648-0188, Fax: 214-648-0167, madhukar.trivedi@utsouthwestern.edu PMCID: PMC5932219 NIHMSID: NIHMS935248 PMID: 29325238 The publisher's version of this article is available at J Clin Psychiatry ### Objective The self-report Concise Associated Symptoms Tracking Scale (CAST-SR) was developed to track mania, irritability, anxiety, panic, and insomnia symptoms among depressed outpatients receiving antidepressant medication. The irritability subscale of the CAST-SR has also been previously associated with hopelessness, a component of suicide risk, and full information about this measure’s development, reliability, and validity among a sample of depressed outpatients has been previously described.4 Originally designed to monitor symptoms among depressed outpatients, the CAST symptom domains may also be useful in monitoring commonly-associated symptoms in other psychiatric conditions that are highly comorbid with depression, like substance use disorders, and are therefore likely to have patients receiving antidepressants as part of their treatment. The current study extends prior psychometric research on the CAST-SR by applying this measure to a sample of antidepressant-medicated individuals with stimulant use disorders receiving health-education or aerobic exercise as part of their participation in a clinical trial. Five factors were determined: mania, irritability, anxiety, panic, and insomnia.4 Stimulant use disorders using DSM-IV criteria were assessed with the clinician-administered World Health Organization (WHO) Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI), Version 2.1.23, 24 Current depressive symptoms were assessed with the 16-item clinician-rated version of the Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology (QIDS-C).25 Adequate levels of reliability (α = .85) and validity have been determined among depressed patients.25 Participants completed the 14-item version of the Concise Health Risk Tracking - Self-Report (CHRT-SR).26 Questions focus on hopelessness, pessimism, perceived lack of social support, passive suicidality, impulsivity, and active suicidal planning and intentions. Furthermore, these results suggest that the CAST-SR reliably measures irritability, insomnia, panic, and anxiety in not only depressed outpatients but also in individuals prescribed antidepressant medications who are also receiving study-based intervention for stimulant-use disorders.

results.title: Psychometrics in Behavioral Software Engineering: A Methodological Introduction with Guidelines
results.content: We detail activities used when operationalizing new psychological constructs, such as item pooling, item review, pilot testing, item analysis, factor analysis, statistical property of items, reliability, validity, and fairness in testing and test bias. With the present article, we are primarily focused on psychological tests, i.e., quantitative research,1 as behavioral software engineering has turned much attention to employing theory and measurement instruments from psychology [14, 30, 42, 54, 80]. Our previous studies have also reported that, when a validated test from psychology is adopted by software engineering researchers, its items are often modified, causing the destruction of its psychometric reliability and validity properties. Gren [56] has also offered a psychological test theory lens for characterizing validity and reliability in behavioral software engineering research, further enforcing our view that software engineering research that investigates any psychological construct quantitatively should maintain fair psychometric properties. After a brief introduction to the key concepts of psychometrics (Section 2) that are required to understand the rest of the article, we focus on test construction in psychometrics and the phases highlighted in Figure 1, namely, pool items (Section 3), item review (Section 4), pilot test (Section 5), item analysis (Section 6), factor analysis (Section 7), statistical properties (Section 8), reliability (Section 9), validity (Section 10), and fairness in testing and test bias (Section 11). Several factors, as defined in the SEPT [3], affect the reliability of a measurement instrument, especially adding or removing items, changing wording or intervals of items, causing variations in the constructs to be measured (e.g., using a measurement instrument for happiness to assess job satisfaction of developers), and ignoring variations in the intended populations for which the test was originally developed. The adoption and development of validated and reliable measurement instruments in software engineering research, whenever humans are to be evaluated, should benefit from psychology and statistics theory; we need not and should not “reinvent the wheel.” This article provides a brief introduction to the evaluation of psychometric tests. After providing basic building blocks and concepts of psychometric theory, we introduced item pooling, item review, pilot testing, item analysis, factor analysis, statistical property of items, reliability, validity, and fairness in testing and test bias.
